title: Q-codes
intro: Three-letter codes starting with Q. Each one is a question when followed by a question mark (QRL?) and a statement without it (QRL). Most come from the ITU list; on the air, hams often use them more loosely.

entries.question: What is the name of your station?
entries.answer: The name of my station is …
entries.usage: Often used for a station's call sign, though the ITU text means the name.

entries.question: How far are you from my station?
entries.answer: The distance between our stations is about …

entries.question: What is my exact frequency?
Does my frequency drift?
How does the tone of my signal sound?
entries.answer: The tone of your signal is …

entries.question: How readable are my signals?
Are you busy?
entries.answer: I am busy, please do not interfere.
entries.usage: QRL? is sent before calling CQ to ask whether the frequency is already in use.

entries.question: Is something interfering with my transmission?
entries.usage: Interference from other stations; hams usually say it about what they hear ("I have QRM").

entries.question: Are you troubled by static?
entries.usage: Atmospheric or natural noise, such as from thunderstorms.

entries.question: Shall I increase my transmitter power?
Shall I reduce my transmitter power?
entries.usage: Also means low-power operating, usually 5 W or less.

entries.question: Shall I send faster?
Shall I send more slowly?
entries.answer: Send more slowly (… words per minute).

entries.question: Shall I stop sending?
entries.usage: "Going QRT" means closing down the station for now.

entries.question: Do you have anything for me?
Are you ready?
entries.usage: Also means active or available on a band ("QRV on 40 m").

entries.question: When will you call me again?
entries.answer: I will call you again at …

entries.question: Who is calling me?
entries.usage: Asks who called; it is not a replacement for CQ.

entries.question: How strong are my signals?
Are my signals fading?
Are my signals garbled?
entries.note: Older lists word it as "Is my keying defective?"

entries.question: Can you hear me between your signals, and may I break in?
entries.answer: I can hear you between my signals; break in.
entries.usage: Full break-in keying: the receiver is heard between the transmitted elements.

entries.question: Can you confirm that you received it?
entries.answer: I confirm that I received it.
entries.usage: "QSL" means confirmed; a QSL card confirms a contact in writing.

entries.question: Can you communicate with … directly or by relay?
entries.answer: I can communicate with … directly (or through …).

entries.question: Will you pass a message on to …?
entries.answer: I will pass it on to …

entries.question: Will you listen for … on … kHz?
entries.answer: I am listening for … on … kHz.
entries.usage: Used in split operation to say where you listen ("QSX 1822").

entries.question: Shall I move to another frequency?
entries.answer: Move to another frequency (or to … kHz).
entries.usage: "QSY to …" means moving to another frequency.

entries.question: Shall I send every word more than once?
How many messages do you have for me?
Where are you located?
entries.usage: "My QTH" is the station's location, usually a town or locator.

entries.question: What is the exact time?

entries.answer: A message for all radio amateurs follows.
entries.note: Amateur usage, mostly in North America. Not in the ITU list.

entries.question: Are you sending with your left foot?
entries.answer: Try sending with your left foot.
entries.note: A joke about poor Morse sending. Not a real Q-code.
